1296.title: Seven points of mind training
1296.hook: Chekawa's seven points, from Atisha's teaching
1296.howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhists of several schools study the Seven Points of Mind Training, memorizing its short slogans and bringing them to mind in daily life, often alongside a teacher's commentary.

segments.voice: Last week, the lamrim, stage by stage, ending with calm, then insight: still the water, then look. A new week starts now.

A monk is visiting someone's room, and on the bed, or the table, lies a short text. He picks it up. Tradition says the lines that caught him asked to take defeat on oneself and offer the victory to others. He couldn't put it down. Who wrote this? Where can I learn it? The monk was Chekawa, and the story goes that he went searching for the teacher behind those lines, and found the teaching had come down from Atisha, quietly, from teacher to student. Later, Chekawa set it out in order, in seven points.
screen: `A SHORT TEXT LEFT ON A TABLE.` → `TAKE DEFEAT, OFFER VICTORY.` → `CHEKAWA GOES LOOKING.`

segments.voice: You met lojong briefly on day three hundred eleven; this week walks it point by point. First, the word. Lojong: lo, mind, and jong, training. Not mind control, not mind emptying. Training, the way a runner trains: the same small moves, done daily, until the body knows them. Second, where it came from. Tibetan tradition says Atisha brought this teaching to Tibet and passed it on to a few close students, almost privately. It was about one thing: turning the mind from caring only for itself toward caring for others, and seeing through the self that does the caring. For a while it traveled by word of mouth. Chekawa, tradition says, gathered it into seven headings so it could be carried. Third, the slogans. Under the headings sit short lines, often called slogans, made to be memorized and pulled out in the middle of a bad day. One asks the student to regard all things as dreams. Another says, in effect, whichever comes, good or bad, be patient. They're short on purpose: you can't recite a long treatise in a traffic jam. Fourth, the seven points. One: the preliminaries, the basics. Two: the main practice, training the awakened heart, including sending and taking. Three: turning bad circumstances into the path. Four: a whole life's practice, gathered into five strengths. Five: how to tell whether the training is working. Six: the commitments. Seven: the guidelines. Today, just the map.
screen: `LOJONG: MIND TRAINING, LIKE A RUNNER.` · `FROM ATISHA, ALMOST PRIVATELY.` · `SHORT SLOGANS FOR A BAD DAY.` · `SEVEN HEADINGS: THE MAP.` · then, large: `SEVEN POINTS.`

segments.voice: Walk through the seven headings slowly, one per breath or two: the basics, the awakened heart, trouble as the path, a whole life's practice, is it working, the commitments, the guidelines. Then try once more with your eyes closed, counting on your fingers; if one slips away, that's fine, just notice which.
Lojong. Mind training: Atisha's teaching on turning toward others, set out by Chekawa in seven points. Today's word.
Your line: seven points. Small enough to count on your fingers. See you at point one.

1297.title: The preliminaries
1297.hook: first point: the four thoughts that turn the mind
1297.howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhist practitioners often begin a session by bringing to mind the four thoughts that turn the mind: precious human life, death and impermanence, karma, and the faults of samsara.

segments.voice: Yesterday, lojong: Chekawa's seven points of mind training. Your line was seven points. Today, point one.

Onions first. Before anything goes in the pan, the cook peels, chops, measures, sets out the salt. Nobody posts a photo of that part. It's slow, it smells, and it isn't the dish. But skip it, and the dish falls apart halfway through, with something burning while you hunt for the garlic. Mind training opens the same way. Before the famous practices, before the slogans about dreams and patience, the very first line of the text says, in effect, start with the groundwork.
screen: `ONIONS FIRST.` → `SKIP IT AND THE DISH FALLS APART.` → `POINT ONE: THE GROUNDWORK.`

segments.voice: First, the slogan. The opening line of the seven points is usually given as: first, train in the preliminaries. The whole rest of the text stands on them. Second, what they are. Tibetan commentaries explain them as four thoughts that turn the mind. One: this human life is precious and hard to come by. Two: it will end, and nobody knows when. Three: actions have results, and they follow you. Four: the round of samsara, however you rearrange it, doesn't satisfy. Third, if that sounds familiar, it should. Last week the lamrim walked through these same four, a day each. Here they come back, packed tight, as the ground floor of mind training, and that repetition is the point. Tibetan teachers say a student doesn't graduate from the preliminaries; the basics get revisited at the start of a session, a day, a hard week. Fourth, why they turn the mind. Picture a cart rolling one way out of habit: toward comfort, distraction, more of the same. The four thoughts are a hand on the shaft, turning it, not by force, but by seeing clearly. If life is precious, short, consequential and not fixable by rearranging, then, in this teaching, training the heart stops looking like a hobby. Only after that turn does Chekawa's text go on to the main practice, and tomorrow, so do these lessons.
screen: `FIRST, TRAIN IN THE PRELIMINARIES.` · `FOUR THOUGHTS THAT TURN THE MIND.` · `THE LAMRIM'S WEEK, PACKED TIGHT.` · `A HAND ON THE CART, TURNING IT.` · then, large: `FIRST THE BASICS.`

segments.voice: Give each of the four thoughts a few slow breaths: this life, precious, rare, here right now; this life, ending, time unknown; what I do, bearing results; the round, unsatisfying however I rearrange it. Don't argue with them or polish them; let each land, like ingredients set out on the counter, and notice whether anything in you turns, even slightly.
The preliminaries. The first of the seven points: four thoughts that turn the mind, the groundwork for everything after. Today's word.
Your line: first the basics. Precious, short, consequential, unsatisfying. Go gently today, and I'll see you tomorrow.

1298.title: Sending and taking
1298.hook: second point: tonglen, riding the breath
1298.howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhist practitioners practice tonglen by imagining taking in others' suffering on the in-breath and sending out happiness on the out-breath, usually beginning with themselves or someone close and widening from there.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the preliminaries: four thoughts that turn the mind, the groundwork of mind training. Your line was first the basics.

Breathe in the good stuff, breathe out the bad. Calm in, stress out. It's the instruction at the end of a yoga class, in a relaxation app, from a kind nurse before a shot, and it makes sense: keep what helps, let go of what hurts. Point two of the seven points of mind training turns it upside down. Breathe in what is heavy, someone's pain, someone's fear. Breathe out whatever is light and good, your ease, your warmth, and send it to them. It sounds backward. It's meant to.
screen: `CALM IN, STRESS OUT.` → `POINT TWO TURNS IT UPSIDE DOWN.` → `TAKE IN THE HEAVY, SEND OUT THE LIGHT.`

segments.voice: You first met tonglen on day three hundred ten; here it sits inside its point. First, the name. Tonglen: tong, sending or giving, and len, taking. It belongs to point two, the main practice, training the awakened heart, the wish to wake up for the sake of others. Second, the instruction. One slogan says, in effect, practice sending and taking alternately, and let the two ride the breath. On the in-breath, the student takes in another's suffering, which some teachers suggest picturing as dark, heavy smoke. On the out-breath, the student sends out happiness, health, whatever good they have, often pictured as cool, bright light. The breath carries it like a horse carries a rider. Third, where to start. Another slogan says to begin the taking with oneself. Teachers suggest starting with your own pain, or the pain of someone you love, before widening to a stranger, and only later to someone difficult. Nobody walks into a gym on the first day and loads the heaviest weight on the rack. Fourth, what it's working on. The habit underneath ordinary life is grab the good, push away the bad. Tonglen trains the opposite reflex, and teachers say what it wears down is self-cherishing, that quiet voice saying me first. It isn't a substitute for actually helping. Practitioners describe it as training the heart, so that when the moment comes to help, the heart is already pointed the right way.
screen: `TONGLEN: SENDING AND TAKING.` · `TAKE IN ON THE BREATH, SEND OUT ON IT.` · `START WITH YOURSELF, THEN WIDEN.` · `IT WEARS DOWN ME FIRST.` · then, large: `RIDING THE BREATH.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something heavy in you right now, a worry, an ache; breathe it in, and on the out-breath send yourself some ease, for a few rounds. Then think of someone you love who's struggling, breathe in their trouble, and breathe out whatever warmth you have toward them. Teachers often give this longer; if it gets too much, come back to just the breath, since nothing is required.
Sending and taking. Tonglen: taking in others' suffering on the in-breath, sending out happiness on the out-breath. Today's word.
Your line: riding the breath. In with the heavy, out with the light. Breathe easy.

1299.title: Bad circumstances as the path
1299.hook: third point: turn difficulties into practice
1299.howItsDone: Practitioners of Tibetan mind training use the slogans of point three in daily life, treating setbacks, illness and difficult people as occasions to practice patience, compassion and letting go of self-cherishing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sending and taking: in with the heavy, out with the light. Your line was riding the breath.

The board flips from delayed to canceled. A groan goes down the gate area. Somebody is already shouting at the agent, who didn't cancel anything. Your phone is at nine percent. The next flight is tomorrow. Two stories are available. In one, the day is ruined, and the path, whatever you were practicing, is on hold until life calms down. In the other, this gate, this groan, this nine percent is the path. Point three of the seven points of mind training picks the second story, on purpose.
screen: `DELAYED. THEN CANCELED.` → `TWO STORIES AVAILABLE.` → `POINT THREE PICKS THE SECOND.`

segments.voice: First, the slogan that opens point three. In effect: when the world is full of trouble, turn every mishap into the path of awakening. Not after the trouble passes; through it. A bad day isn't a break from practice. It's the material. Second, where the blame goes. Another slogan says to drive all blame into one. That one isn't the agent, and it isn't you as a person to be beaten up. In the commentaries it's self-cherishing, the me-first reflex that turns every delay into a personal insult. The trouble may be real; the commentaries trace the extra misery to that reflex. Third, gratitude, of all things. Another slogan says to be grateful to everyone. The commentaries explain that a person who tests your patience gives you a chance to practice it that an easy person never could. A story told about Atisha, which you met on day nine hundred sixty-nine, says he brought a difficult, short-tempered attendant with him to Tibet, and when asked why, called him his teacher of patience. Fourth, what this is not. It isn't a teaching to stay where you're being harmed, or to call injustice fine. You can leave the gate, rebook, speak up; point three is about the mind that goes with you while you do. If someone is hurting you, you deserve safety: call local emergency help, or in the US, call or text 988. And yesterday's tonglen fits here: breathe in the frustration of the whole gate, breathe out a little patience toward everyone stuck with you, including the agent.

segments.voice: Bring to mind a small annoyance from the last day or two, a splinter, not a big wound, and let it play once, noticing where the me-first reflex shows up: why me, how dare they. Then try two moves from point three: point the blame at that reflex instead of at the person, and look for one thing the annoyance is teaching, patience, slowing down, anything.
Bad circumstances as the path. The third of the seven points: trouble isn't an interruption of practice; it's the practice. Today's word.

1300.title: Five strengths
1300.hook: fourth point: a lifetime's practice in five strengths: intention, familiarity, seed, reproach, aspiration
1300.howItsDone: Practitioners of Tibetan mind training use the five strengths to frame a day: setting an intention in the morning, practicing and doing good through the day, rejecting self-cherishing when it arises, and making an aspiration and dedication at night.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bad circumstances as the path. Your line was trouble is the path.

A toothbrush is a lifetime practice nobody calls spiritual. Twice a day, for decades, mostly without thinking, and it works because it's small and it never stops. How does anyone keep a deep practice going for a whole life, through jobs and moves and grief and boredom? The honest answer usually isn't a dramatic vow. It's something closer to the toothbrush. Point four of the seven points of mind training gathers a whole life's practice into a short list a person can actually carry.
screen: `A TOOTHBRUSH, TWICE A DAY.` → `HOW DO YOU KEEP IT UP FOR LIFE?` → `POINT FOUR: A SHORT LIST.`

segments.voice: First, intention. The strength of resolve: setting the mind, at the start of the day, the week, the year, on the awakened heart. Something like: today, as far as I can, I won't lose sight of others. The aim, chosen ahead of time. Second, familiarity: doing it again and again until it's ordinary. The commentaries on mind training say that whatever the mind gets used to becomes easy. Third, the seed, sometimes called the white seed: doing good, small and concrete, so the practice has something to grow from. Not big gestures. A kindness, a gift, a held door. Fourth, reproach. This one can sound harsh. It means turning against self-cherishing whenever it shows up, the me-first reflex from yesterday, and saying to it plainly: you're the troublemaker here. Not shame aimed at yourself; a firm no aimed at a habit. Fifth, aspiration. At the end of the day, a wish, often made with a dedication of whatever good was done: that it go toward the welfare of all beings, and that this training continue. So the day has a shape. Intention in the morning. Familiarity and seed through the day. Reproach when the old reflex flares. Aspiration at night. Tibetan tradition also teaches the same five strengths for the time of dying, so the practice a person has lived with is the practice they die with. Five words, held lightly, for a whole life.

1301.title: Two witnesses
1301.hook: fifth point: of the two witnesses, others' opinion and your own, trust your own honest one
1301.howItsDone: Practitioners of Tibetan mind training assess their practice by point five's measures, chiefly whether self-cherishing is lessening, and rely on their own honest self-examination rather than others' praise or blame.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the five strengths: intention, familiarity, seed, reproach, aspiration. Your line was five strengths.

Four and a half stars. A restaurant, a plumber, a podcast, a person's whole social feed: a lot of daily life runs on the ratings of strangers. And it spills over. Did that go well? Check the reactions. Am I a good person? Look at how many people seem to think so. Every practice reaches this question sooner or later: how would you know it's working? Point five of the seven points of mind training gives several answers, and one of them puts the ratings in their place.
screen: `FOUR AND A HALF STARS.` → `LIVING BY STRANGERS' RATINGS.` → `HOW WOULD YOU KNOW IT'S WORKING?`

segments.voice: First, one measure. A slogan of point five says, in effect, that all the teachings agree at one point. The commentaries name it: is self-cherishing getting smaller? Not visions, not hours logged. Is the me-first reflex a little quieter than it was? Second, the two witnesses. One is other people's opinion of you; the other is your own. The slogan says to hold the principal one, and the commentaries say the principal one is your own. Others see only the outside. They can be fooled by a calm face, and miss a quiet effort entirely. Only the one acting was there for the motive: the flash of envy let go, the kindness done partly for show. Third, the honest witness. This isn't permission to grade yourself kindly; the witness has to be honest, or it's just a fan. The older suttas have a picture for it, the one you met on day three hundred sixty-eight. In a discourse to his son Rahula, the Buddha compares checking an action to looking in a mirror: before you act, while you act, and after, ask whether it harms yourself or others. A mirror doesn't flatter and doesn't scold. It shows. Fourth, two other signs from point five. One slogan says to keep a joyful mind, steady rather than giddy. Another says that if you can practice even when distracted, you are well trained, the way a good rider stays on when the horse shies. None of these need an audience. Others' praise is pleasant; others' blame stings. Neither is the witness that counts here.
screen: `ONE MEASURE: LESS ME FIRST.` · `TWO WITNESSES: THEIRS AND YOURS.` · `THE HONEST WITNESS IS A MIRROR.` · `JOY, AND PRACTICE WHEN DISTRACTED.` · then, large: `YOUR OWN WITNESS.`

segments.voice: Pick one moment from the past day, something you said or did with another person, and hold it up like a mirror: what did it look like from outside, and what was underneath it, the real motive, as best you can see it? Don't defend it and don't punish it. Then ask the one question point five cares about: was the me-first reflex louder or quieter then?
Two witnesses. Others' opinion of you, and your own honest one. Point five says to hold your own. Today's word.

1302.title: Commitments
1302.hook: sixth point: don't speak of others' faults, don't wait in ambush, don't be fickle
1302.howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhists who practice mind training (lojong) study the seven points with a teacher and often recite or reflect on their short lines, including the commitments of the sixth point, as reminders through the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, two witnesses: what others say about you, and what you honestly know. Your line: your own witness.

Somebody's name comes up at lunch. They aren't there. Within a minute the table has a verdict on them, and it isn't kind. Nobody planned it; it just happens, the way water runs downhill. The old Tibetan mind-training teachings know that table well. Their sixth point is a set of commitments, short lines to live by, and a few could have been written for that lunch. Don't talk about other people's faults. Don't wait in ambush. Don't be fickle. Today, the promises that keep mind training honest.
screen: `A NAME COMES UP AT LUNCH.` → `THE SIXTH POINT: COMMITMENTS.` → `PROMISES THAT KEEP IT HONEST.`

segments.voice: First, what a commitment is here. Tibetan tradition credits the seven points of mind training to the teacher Chekawa, who gathered teachings it traces back to Atisha. The sixth point is a list of commitments: not laws handed down from above, but promises a student keeps so the practice doesn't quietly turn sour. Second, don't speak of others' faults. The Dhammapada puts the problem plainly, in Max Müller's translation: "The fault of others is easily perceived, but that of oneself is difficult to perceive." Pointing out someone's weakness can feel like insight. Often it's a way of not looking at your own. Third, don't wait in ambush, your line today. It means not storing up a hurt and keeping it ready for the right moment to pay someone back. A grudge can be very patient. The commitment asks you to put it down quietly, when nobody would ever know you had it. Fourth, don't be fickle. Translators render it in different ways, but the sense is steadiness: not warm one day and cold the next. Kindness that depends on your mood hasn't been trained yet. Now the week: the preliminaries, first the basics. Sending and taking, riding the breath. Trouble as the path. Five strengths. Two witnesses. And today, commitments. One point is left, guidelines, and the seven are complete. Notice where all of them aim: at your own mind, not at the person who isn't at the table.
screen: `PROMISES, NOT LAWS.` · `OTHERS' FAULTS ARE EASY TO SEE.` · `DON'T KEEP A HURT READY.` · `STEADY, NOT WARM AND COLD.` · then, large: `DON'T WAIT IN AMBUSH.`

segments.voice: Pick one of today's three, not speaking of a fault, not waiting in ambush, not blowing hot and cold, and bring to mind one person it touches: someone whose faults you could list without trying, or someone you've been quietly saving something for. Hold them in mind and keep the promise: no case against them, no plan. If an old grievance rises, let it sit there, unused.
Commitments. The sixth point of mind training: promises a student keeps, like not speaking of others' faults and not waiting in ambush. Today's word.
Your line: don't wait in ambush. Promises, not laws, kept for your own mind's sake. Back tomorrow, same hill.
